LAREDO — District 8 Council Member Alyssa Cigarroa is asking voters to make her mayor on November 3. Her campaign's 30th-day-before-election finance report — the last full look at her money before Election Day — was filed with the City Secretary and posted on the City of Laredo's campaign finance reports page under the October 5, 2026 deadline, in two parts. It is a public record, and it answers a question every voter is entitled to ask: who is paying for this campaign?

The headline numbers

Between July 1 and September 24, 2026, the campaign reported $374,500 in total contributions — $364,600 itemized across 133 contributors, plus $9,900 in in-kind support — against $295,692.14 in expenditures, leaving $77,195 in the bank at the end of the period and no outstanding loans. Her campaign treasurer of record is Ricardo Sandoval, who also appears in the filing as a $10,000 contributor himself. And one figure repeated in posts circulating this week does not survive the document: the Killam support totals $29,900 in the filing, not the $39,900 being shared.

The names on the filing

The contributions itemized in the report read like a directory of Laredo's oldest family names. Grouped by family, the largest totals in the filing are: the Cigarroa family, $73,250 — including $50,000 from Dr. Ricardo Cigarroa alone, in two contributions of $25,000 each; the Killam family and its companies, $29,900 — $20,000 in contributions from Killam Development LTD and David Killam, plus $9,900 in billboards Killam Development donated in kind; the Deutsch family, $18,000; and $10,000 each from Evelyn A. Sames, from Leila R. Martin of San Antonio, and from Betty Bruni Moreno, plus $5,000 from the Arguindegui family. Individual entries include $10,000 from Jose Carlos Casanova on August 12, 2026, $10,000 from Killam Development LTD on September 10, 2026, $5,000 from Cindy E. Cantu on September 10, 2026, $5,000 from Richard Lange of El Paso, $5,000 from LSMC Investments LLC, and $1,000 plus $4,000 from Patricia Keck and her husband Ray. None of that is illegal — Texas sets no contribution limits in local races, and every dollar was disclosed, as the law requires. But disclosure exists so voters can judge for themselves whose support a candidate carries into office.

A medical family, on the record

Cigarroa's own name is the biggest one on that list, and her family is not just a Laredo family — it is a Laredo medical institution. Laredo Medical Center is home to the Cigarroa Heart and Vascular Institute, where cardiologist Dr. Ricardo G. Cigarroa practices; the hospital's own newsroom welcomed his son, Dr. Ricardo J.G. Cigarroa II, to its medical staff in 2020, noting his office at the institute. A federal court order in the antitrust case Doctors Hospital of Laredo v. Cigarroa describes Dr. Ricardo Cigarroa, his son, and his nephew Dr. Joaquin Cigarroa practicing together at the institute and Laredo Medical Center; the case ended in January 2025 with summary judgment for the defendants. Her extended family also includes Dr. Francisco G. Cigarroa, the Laredo-born pediatric transplant surgeon who served as chancellor of the University of Texas System, and Patricia Cigarroa Keck, wife of former Texas A&M International University president Dr. Ray Keck.

The hospital question

That family history is why one line on a recent council agenda matters. The September 21, 2026 City Council agenda — in the section of items requested by Council Member Alyssa Cigarroa — carried item 26-C-154: discussion of "the non-binding pediatric hospital ballot referendum, including consideration of a funding mechanism to be adopted contingent upon voter approval." Ballotpedia lists the measure on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 1, an advisory measure asking whether the city should expand pediatric hospital services. An advisory vote binds no one, and the agenda item names no tax — but it leaves open a "funding mechanism" to be named later, for a children's hospital in a city where the candidate's family name is on a hospital institute. Voters are entitled to ask what that mechanism would be, and who would run what it funds.

For the record: the pediatric hospital push did not start with Cigarroa. On June 24, 2024, the council unanimously approved Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño's request to seek voter approval for a pediatric hospital bond election. The children's hospital did not appear as its own proposition in the May 3, 2025 bond election; that $417 million package — $271.1 million for public safety, $70.8 million for public health, $65 million for streets, and $10 million for the Hamilton Senior Apartments — was approved by the council to go before voters. Webb Watch found no record of Cigarroa voting against the bond package, and no official document proposing a "medical district tax." Claims circulating about either point should be treated as unproven unless a record is produced.

One name we could not confirm

The filing's $5,000 entry from Cindy E. Cantu has been accompanied online by a claim that she is the wife of Municipal Court Judge Jesus "Chuy" Dominguez — who, according to his own city filing, now holds that court and is seeking the 111th District Court bench. Webb Watch could not confirm that relationship from any reputable source, and public records searches associate a Laredo woman of that name with a different spouse. Until a reliable source confirms it, that claim is not verified, and we are not stating it as fact.

The bottom line

A campaign finance report is not an accusation. It is a list of names and numbers that the law makes public precisely so voters can weigh them. Cigarroa's filing shows a campaign carried heavily by Laredo's established families — including her own, whose name is attached to one of the city's two hospitals — at the same moment she has put a children's-hospital referendum, and an unnamed funding mechanism behind it, on the council's table. Whether that is a coalition or a conflict is a judgment the report leaves, properly, to the voters of Laredo.

title: Follow the Money: Who Is Financing Alyssa Cigarroa's Run for Mayor?
